claim: CD8lumenal consists of a signal sequence, a fluorescent protein (GFP or DsRed), four repeats of an FM domain (FM4), and the CD8 protein.
source: As the basic unit of a lumenal membrane staple we designed a chimeric protein, termed CD8lumenal, that contained a signal sequence, for its proper insertion and translocation across the ER membrane, fused to 1) a fluorescent protein (GFP or DsRed) to track the protein within the cells by confocal microscopy, 2) four repeats of a domain (FM4) designed to self-aggregate in trans in the absence of the disaggregating drug (AP21998) (Rollins et al., 2000), and 3) the CD8 protein, known to be a trans-membrane protein ultimately targeted to the plasma membrane (Hennecke and Cosson, 1993; Lavieu et al., 2010).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the composition of the CD8lumenal construct and cites prior work establishing the properties of its components.

claim: FM4 domains self-aggregate in trans in the absence of the disaggregating drug AP21998.
source: four repeats of a domain (FM4) designed to self-aggregate in trans in the absence of the disaggregating drug (AP21998) (Rollins et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rollins et al., 2000.

claim: CD8 is a trans-membrane protein ultimately targeted to the plasma membrane.
source: the CD8 protein, known to be a trans-membrane protein ultimately targeted to the plasma membrane (Hennecke and Cosson, 1993; Lavieu et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hennecke and Cosson, 1993 and Lavieu et al., 2010.

claim: The intra-lumenal separation between stapled membranes could vary from 10 to 23 nm depending on the arrangement of trans-aggregating FM4 domains.
source: These staples are expected to remain in the ER if they are planar and too large to be packaged into a small COPII vesicle. Various structural models suggest a planar adhesion plaque will form that closely links two sides of ER lamellae or tubules, with an intra-lumenal separation between the stapled membranes that from first principles could vary from 10 to 23 nm (Figure 1A), depending on the preferred arrangement of trans-aggregating FM4 domains.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling shown in Figure 1A and inference from structural principles.

claim: If repeat FM domains interact like cadherins primarily via their most-membrane distant module, the membrane separation in the stapled state would be close to 25 nm.
source: In particular, however, if repeat FM domains interact like cadherins (Miyaguchi, 2000; Pokutta and Weis, 2007) primarily via their most-membrane distant module (i.e., at their tips), then we would expect a membrane separation in the stapled state close to 25 nm (model 1 in Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cadherin behavior (cited) and structural modeling shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ER-aggregated CD8lumenal forms electron-dense flat features visible by electron microscopy.
source: When CD8lumenal is expressed in HeLa cells in the absence of the disaggregating drug AP21998, numerous, discrete electron-dense plaques are in fact readily observed by electron microscopy (Figure 1B, red square).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lumenal staples trigger lumenal constrictions within ER tubules with a separation averaging 25 ± 5 nm.
source: The staples trigger lumenal constrictions within ER tubules (Figure 1C) whose separation averages 25 ± 5 nm, suggesting that model 1 in which only the distal FM domains are typically bonded prevails in the ER (Figure 1A) most closely approximates the structure of the adhesion plaque.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cytosolic staples trigger artificial stacking of ER membranes.
source: Remarkably, when we used cytosolic staples that harbor the FM domains at the cytosolic face of the membranes (CD8cytosolic), ER membranes were artificially stacked, confirming the trans–nature of the staples interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD8lumenal is transported to the cell surface only when AP21998 is added to disaggregate the staples in the ER.
source: Only when AP21998 is added to disaggregate the staples in the ER is CD8lumenal transported to the cell surface (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ER staples do not prevent the production or transport of co-expressed Golgi resident enzymes.
source: Importantly, when the staples are stuck in the ER they did not prevent the production or transport of co-expressed Golgi resident enzymes (ST-RFP), showing that ER staples are not toxic (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating normal ST-RFP localization.

claim: Treatment with disaggregating drug for 4 hours increases TritonX-100 solubility of CD8lumenal by a factor of 3.9 ± 0.9.
source: When tested by SDS-PAGE, the disaggregating drug increased Triton-X100 solubility (without sonication procedure) of CD8lumenal in cell extracts by a factor 3.9 ± 0.9 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Disaggregated CD8lumenal shows reduced mobility on SDS-PAGE gel.
source: Disaggregated CD8lumenal, expected to be O-glycosylated (Nilsson et al., 1989; Lavieu et al., 2010), appeared as an isoform with reduced SDS-PAGE motility (* Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C and citations to prior work on O-glycosylation.

claim: Jacalin exclusively precipitates disaggregated CD8lumenal.
source: As expected, Jacalin, a lectin that binds D-Galactose residues, exclusively precipitates this isoform (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Staples have a half-life of approximately 5.5 hours.
source: In addition, metabolic radiolabeling experiments showed that staples (∼5.5 hr half-life) were slightly more stable that disaggregated CD8lumenal (∼2.5 hr half-life) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolic radiolabeling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Disaggregated CD8lumenal has a half-life of approximately 2.5 hours.
source: In addition, metabolic radiolabeling experiments showed that staples (∼5.5 hr half-life) were slightly more stable that disaggregated CD8lumenal (∼2.5 hr half-life) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolic radiolabeling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 16°C temperature block slows export of secretory cargo from the ER but slows anterograde transport in the Golgi stack even more, resulting in accumulation in the ERGIC and cis-most Golgi cisterna.
source: Temperature blocks in the 15–18°C range slow export of secretory cargo from the ER, but slow anterograde transport in the Golgi stack even more, resulting in limited penetration of the Golgi stack with accumulation in the ER–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) and the cis-most Golgi cisterna or two (Hobman et al., 1992; Balch et al., 1994; Volchuk et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hobman et al., 1992; Balch et al., 1994; Volchuk et al., 2000).

claim: CD8lumenal re-aggregated in the Golgi at 16°C does not reach the cell surface and is retained in the Golgi.
source: Surprisingly, the CD8lumenal re-aggregated in the Golgi at 16°C did not reach the surface and was retained in the Golgi as judged by confocal microscopy (Figure 3B,C, lane 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface biotinylation and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Golgi retention of staples is due to controlled aggregation and is removed when the disaggregating drug is added back.
source: Golgi retention of the staples is due to controlled aggregation, because this block to transport was removed when the drug was added back, and CD8lumenal (disaggregated) now moves from the Golgi to the plasma membrane (Figure 3B,C, lane 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface biotinylation and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Helix Pomatia precipitates a portion of disaggregated CD8lumenal at 16°C.
source: Specifically, a portion of disaggregated CD8lumenal is precipitated by Helix Pomatia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a lectin that binds a N-Acetyl-Galactosamine residue that is only added within the cis-Golgi (Roth et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by lectin precipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Roth et al., 1994.

claim: Jacalin does not precipitate CD8lumenal at 16°C.
source: In contrast, the lectin Jacalin, which requires trans-Golgi localized modifications for binding (Spicer and Schulte, 1992), did not precipitate CD8lumenal at 16°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although it did at 37°C (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by lectin precipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Spicer and Schulte, 1992.

claim: Membrane staples formed at 16°C co-localize with cis-Golgi marker Grasp65 but not with trans-Golgi marker Golgin97.
source: Using the same method we demonstrated that the initial localization of membrane staples Golgi staples formed at 16°C overlaps with the cis- but not the trans-Golgi marker. This co-localization with the cis- but not the trans-Golgi marker persists following warm-up to 20°C (Figure 4B, 2, 3 and graph), implying that the staples do not migrate in the cis → trans direction within the stack, even under conditions where this transport process is expected to resume.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and Pearson's coefficient analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Staples do not migrate in the cis → trans direction within the stack following warm-up to 20°C.
source: This co-localization with the cis- but not the trans-Golgi marker persists following warm-up to 20°C (Figure 4B, 2, 3 and graph), implying that the staples do not migrate in the cis → trans direction within the stack, even under conditions where this transport process is expected to resume.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating persistent cis-Golgi localization.

claim: Staples formed at 16°C and chased at 20°C are exclusively localized at one face of the Golgi, within the very first or more rarely the second and third cisternae.
source: Staples formed at 16°C and then chased at 20°C for either 2 or 6 hr (which according to confocal microscopy remained in the cis-Golgi) were as would now be expected exclusively localized at one face of the Golgi, within the very first or more rarely the second and the third cisternae (Figure 5A–C and graph Figure 7C for quantification).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A–C and quantification in Figure 7C.

claim: Staples span a gap of 27 ± 3 nm between opposing membrane surfaces within Golgi cisternae.
source: The staples were recognized in thin sections as electron dense plaques within Golgi cisternae (arrows, Figure 5A–C) spanning a gap of 27 ± 3 nm (Figure 5D) between opposing membrane surfaces, similar to their morphology within the ER.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Gold particles recognizing GFP harbored by staples co-localize with gold particles that bind GM130, a cis-Golgi marker.
source: Immuno-electron microscopy established that this face is the cis-Golgi since the gold particles recognizing the GFP harbored by the staples co-localized with the gold particles that bind GM130, a cis-Golgi marker (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immuno-electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Staples are at the opposed end of the stack from clathrin, which is a trans-Golgi marker.
source: Confirming this, the staples were at the opposed end of the stack from clathrin, which is a trans-Golgi marker (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immuno-electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Staples formed at 16°C and chased at 20°C harbor a cis-glycan signature but not the trans-glycan signature.
source: Consistently, lectin-precipitation experiment showed that staples formed at 16°C and chased at 20°C harbored a cis-glycan signature (precipitated by Helix pomatis) but not the trans-glycan signature (not precipitated by Jacalin) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, lane 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by lectin precipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Staples accumulate at the central portion of the cis-most cisternae being excluded from their rims.
source: Interestingly, the staples accumulate at the central portion of the cis-most cisternae (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) being excluded from their rims.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Staples preferentially form in the flattened central regions of a cisterna because they are too small to fit across a dilated rim.
source: This could be the consequence of the fixed dimension of the staples, which are too small to fit across a dilated rim (Figure 5D). So, the staples would be expected to preferentially form in the flattened central regions of a cisterna.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural constraints shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Staples formed at 20°C remain at the Golgi even after cells are warmed up to 37°C for 2 hours.
source: Surface biotinylation established that staples formed at 20°C remained at the Golgi even after the cells were warmed up to 37°C for 2 hr (Figure 5G), similar to the cis-Golgi staples.
evidence: The claim is supported by surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Staples formed at 20°C are present and retained throughout the entire Golgi stack, including the trans-most Golgi cisterna.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that the staples formed at 20°C were present and retained throughout the entire Golgi stack, including the trans-most Golgi cisterna (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The amount of VSV-G detected at the surface of cells that harbored staples in their Golgi was 91 ± 12% of the amount detected at the surface of cells harboring a normal Golgi.
source: Surface biotinylation showed that the amount of VSV-G detected at the surface of cells that harbored staples in their Golgi was 91 ± 12% of the amount of VSV-G detected at the surface of cells harboring a normal Golgi (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The rate of release of PA-GFP-VSV-G from long-term stapled Golgi is indistinguishable from that measured from a non-stapled Golgi.
source: The rate of the release (half-time ∼ 5 min) of PA-GFP-VSV-G from even long-term (4 hr) stapled Golgi was indistinguishable from that measured from a non-stapled Golgi identified with a red-tagged Golgi marker (ST-RFP) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by photo-activation experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cells harboring stapled-Golgi for 2 hours showed 92.5 ± 13% of freshly secreted collagen-I when compared to cells harboring normal Golgi.
source: Cells harboring stapled-Golgi for 2 hr showed 92.5 ± 13% of freshly secreted collagen-I when compared to cells harboring normal Golgi (set to 100%).
evidence: The claim is supported by TCA precipitation/immunoblotting data described in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The kinetics of secretion for collagen-I and MMP2 do not show robust differences whether the Golgi apparatus is stapled or not.
source: To rigorously assess if Golgi staples had only minor effect on secretion, we further tested the rate of transport of collagen-I and MMP2, two proteins secreted by Saos-2 cells. The kinetics of secretion for both proteins did not show any robust differences whether the Golgi apparatus was stapled or not (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic secretion data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Redistribution of Golgi enzymes into the ER under BFA treatment occurs whether Golgi staples are present or not.
source: To further test if Golgi staples interfere with the behavior of Golgi membranes, we assessed the redistribution of Golgi resident enzymes into the ER under BFA treatment (Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 1989). Redistribution of Golgi enzymes into the ER was observed whether Golgi staples were present or not (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and citation to Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 1989.

claim: Staples readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes and do not perturb the diffusion of Golgi resident enzymes.
source: Importantly, FRAP experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) showed that staples (localized either within the Golgi or within the ER) readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes and do not perturb the diffusion of Golgi resident enzymes; in fact, Golgi-staples diffused only slightly more slowly than disaggregated CD8lumenal at 20°C (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: When soluble FM4 and membrane-bound FM4 proteins are present in the ER they are efficiently co-immunoprecipitated from cell extracts.
source: As expected, when the two FM-containing proteins were present in the ER they were efficiently co-immunoprecipitated from cell extracts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: When soluble FM4 and membrane-bound FM4 proteins are disaggregated and allowed to leave the ER and then re-aggregated in the cis-Golgi at 16°C, the Golgi-modified forms are no longer co-immunoprecipitated.
source: However, when these same proteins were disaggregated and allowed to leave the ER and then re-aggregated for 1 hr in the cis-Golgi at 16°C, or even further in the Golgi stack at 20°C, the Golgi-modified forms of these same proteins were no longer co-immunoprecipitated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Homo-aggregates constituted of soluble cargo (hGH) are efficiently formed even after re-aggregation at 16°C or 20°C.
source: On the contrary homo-aggregates constituted of soluble cargo (hGH) were efficiently formed even after re-aggregation at 16°C or 20°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Soluble and membrane-bound FM proteins segregate into separate aggregates within the same Golgi area.
source: Confocal microscopy independently established that the soluble and membrane-bound FM proteins segregated into separate aggregates within the same Golgi area (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and, electron microscopy confirmed that this separation occurs even within the same cisternal compartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and electron microscopy data.

claim: Within the same cisterna, electron-dense plaques comprising the staples are localized in the central regions while soluble aggregates are concentrated at the dilated rims.
source: Even when both reside in the same cisterna, the electron-dense plaques comprising the staples are localized in the central regions of the cisterna while the soluble aggregates are concentrated at the dilated rims (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: DsRed-hGH is secreted regardless of its own re-aggregation status or the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal.
source: Immunoblot, after surface biotinylation and TCA precipitation of the media, showing that DsRed-hGH is secreted regardless of its own re-aggregation status, or the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When aggregates accumulated in the cis-Golgi are allowed to move anterograde through but not exit the Golgi following warm-up to 20°C, approximately 75% of the staples remain at the cis-face of the Golgi.
source: When aggregates accumulated in the cis-Golgi are allowed to move anterograde through but not exit the Golgi following warm-up to 20°C, ≈75% of the staples, as expected, remain at the cis-face of the Golgi, whereas ≈75% of the soluble aggregates are transported to the opposite, trans-face of the same Golgi stacks (Figure 7B and graph).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 7B and graph.

claim: When aggregates accumulated in the cis-Golgi are allowed to move anterograde through but not exit the Golgi following warm-up to 20°C, approximately 75% of the soluble aggregates are transported to the trans-face of the same Golgi stacks.
source: When aggregates accumulated in the cis-Golgi are allowed to move anterograde through but not exit the Golgi following warm-up to 20°C, ≈75% of the staples, as expected, remain at the cis-face of the Golgi, whereas ≈75% of the soluble aggregates are transported to the opposite, trans-face of the same Golgi stacks (Figure 7B and graph).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 7B and graph.

claim: Membrane staples localize to the central regions of Golgi cisternae where they segregate from large soluble aggregates which mainly concentrate at the dilated rims.
source: With this in mind, our findings can be simply summarized as follows: 1) membrane staples localize to the central regions of Golgi cisternae where they segregate from large soluble aggregates which mainly concentrate at the dilated rims; and 2) membrane staples remain in place as anterograde transport occurs, whereas large soluble aggregates and small cargo are transported at normal rates.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings supported by multiple data sources including electron microscopy and confocal microscopy.

claim: Membrane staples remain in place as anterograde transport occurs, whereas large soluble aggregates and small cargo are transported at normal rates.
source: With this in mind, our findings can be simply summarized as follows: 1) membrane staples localize to the central regions of Golgi cisternae where they segregate from large soluble aggregates which mainly concentrate at the dilated rims; and 2) membrane staples remain in place as anterograde transport occurs, whereas large soluble aggregates and small cargo are transported at normal rates.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings supported by multiple data sources including surface biotinylation, electron microscopy, and photo-activation experiments.

claim: While the cisternae are static on the time scale of protein traffic, the dilated rims are mobile and progress in the cis → trans direction via a mechanism termed 'Rim Progression'.
source: The obvious explanation of the above is that while the cisternae in the stack (containing staples mainly in their central regions) are static, the rims of cisternae—mainly containing the soluble aggregates—are mobile (at least on the average) in the anterograde direction, a process we term 'rim progression'.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data, representing the authors' proposed model based on their experimental findings.

claim: The strongest evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks is that intrinsically large soluble cargoes such as immature collagen aggregates can be rapidly transported across the stack.
source: The strongest evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks is that intrinsically large soluble cargoes such as immature collagen aggregates (Bonfanti et al., 1998)—which are far too large to be accommodated by COPI transport vesicles—can nonetheless be rapidly transported across the stack.
evidence: The claim cites prior work (Bonfanti et al., 1998) as evidence for cisternal progression.

claim: A 20°C temperature block slows exit from the trans-most Golgi cisterna (TGN) more than it slows ER → Golgi transport or transport from cis → trans Golgi.
source: A classic example is the 20°C temperature block, which slows exit from the trans-most Golgi cisterna (TGN) more than it slows ER → Golgi transport or transport from cis → trans Golgi (Matlin and Simons, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Matlin and Simons, 1983.

claim: Approximately 20% of collagen aggregates remain in the Golgi cisternae, mainly in the centers of the cisternae.
source: A striking feature of the collagen data is that while the majority of the aggregates are indeed rapidly transported, a sizable minority (∼20% [Bonfanti et al., 1998]) remains in the Golgi cisternae, mainly in the centers of the cisternae, consistent with our results and interpretation.
evidence: The claim cites data from Bonfanti et al., 1998 and relates it to the current findings.

claim: In budding yeast, the process of cisternal maturation is well documented.
source: In budding yeast, where cisternae generally do not stack, the process of cisternal maturation is well documented, though formal proof that anterograde cargo is present in maturing cisternae is still lacking (Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Losev et al., 2006 and Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006.

claim: COPI vesicles bud extensively from the rims of Golgi cisternae at every level and contain both retrograde-directed cargo and anterograde-directed cargo such as insulin, albumin, and VSV-G.
source: COPI vesicles are known to bud extensively from the rims of Golgi cisternae at every level and contain–in addition to retrograde-directed cargo–anterograde-directed cargo such as insulin, albumin, and VSV-G (Rothman, 2010); so this biochemically well-understood pathway (Popoff et al., 2011) would seem to be the principal contender.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rothman, 2010 and Popoff et al., 2011.
